title: Transmission Fluid Leak: Red Fluid Causes & Fixes
h1: Transmission Fluid Leak? Why There's Red Fluid Under Your Car
metaDescription: Reddish fluid under your car and rough shifts? Learn what causes transmission leaks, how serious low fluid is, and what to check before damage sets in.
intro: A thin, reddish or light-brown fluid - sometimes smelling slightly sweet or burnt - usually points to a transmission fluid leak. Your transmission relies on this fluid for both lubrication and hydraulic pressure, so running low can cause slipping, harsh or delayed shifts, and eventually serious internal damage. Most leaks come from a worn pan gasket, a seal, or a line rather than the transmission itself, which makes catching it early important.

commonCauses.detail: The pan holds the fluid and its gasket is a frequent leak point; a damaged pan, worn gasket, or loose bolts let fluid drip from under the transmission.

commonCauses.cause: Worn axle, output, or input shaft seals
commonCauses.detail: Rubber seals where shafts exit the transmission harden and leak with age and heat, often dripping toward the front or sides of the vehicle.
Metal or rubber lines run fluid to a cooler in the radiator; corroded lines, cracked rubber sections, or loose fittings leak, sometimes near the radiator.

commonCauses.cause: Torque converter or front pump seal
commonCauses.detail: A leaking converter seal or cracked converter drips at the bell housing between the engine and transmission - a more involved repair.
Heavy use or towing can overheat the transmission, loosening seals and pushing fluid past them; an overfilled transmission can also force fluid out the vent.

commonCauses.cause: Loose or missing drain plug / fill plug
commonCauses.detail: On transmissions with a drain plug, an improperly tightened plug or worn washer leaks slowly after a service.

whatToDo: Low transmission fluid can permanently damage the transmission, so don't drive far on a noticeable leak. Check the fluid (many cars have a transmission dipstick - check warm and running per your owner's manual) and note its color: pink/red is fine, dark brown or burnt-smelling means it's overdue for service. If shifting is slipping or harsh, or fluid is dripping steadily, get it to a shop before driving more, since continuing on low fluid is what turns a cheap gasket job into a transmission rebuild.

title: Car AC Not Blowing Cold Air? Top Causes & Fixes
h1: Car A/C Not Blowing Cold? Here's Why and How to Fix It
metaDescription: AC blowing warm air? Learn the most common reasons your car's A/C stopped cooling - from low refrigerant to a bad compressor - and what to do next.
intro: When your A/C blows warm or room-temperature air, the system has usually lost its ability to remove heat from the cabin - most often because it's low on refrigerant due to a small leak. Other culprits include a failed compressor or clutch, a clogged or damaged condenser, or an electrical fault that keeps the compressor from turning on. It's almost never a safety issue, but on a hot day it's miserable, and some causes get worse and more expensive the longer you wait.

commonCauses.detail: The most common cause. The A/C system is sealed, so if refrigerant is low there's a leak - commonly at O-rings, the Schrader valve service ports, hose connections, the condenser, or the evaporator. Low charge often stops the compressor from engaging at all.
The compressor pumps refrigerant; a seized compressor or a clutch that won't engage means no cooling. A clutch rapidly cycling on and off every few seconds usually signals low refrigerant.
Mounted in front of the radiator, the condenser is exposed to road debris; a puncture causes a leak, and bent fins or blockage reduce its ability to shed heat.

commonCauses.cause: Electrical fault - relay, fuse, or pressure switch
commonCauses.detail: A blown fuse, bad A/C relay or clutch relay, or a faulty refrigerant pressure sensor can cut power to the compressor so it never turns on.

commonCauses.cause: Blend door or HVAC control problem
commonCauses.detail: A stuck blend-door actuator can route warm air past the evaporator, so the system cools but warm air still reaches the vents.

commonCauses.cause: Failed blower motor or clogged cabin filter
commonCauses.detail: Weak airflow (rather than warm air) can come from a dying blower motor or a clogged cabin air filter restricting airflow over the evaporator.

whatToDo: This is safe to drive with - it's a comfort issue, not a hazard. Start with the easy checks: confirm the A/C is actually set to cold/recirculate, check the cabin air filter, and listen for the compressor clutch clicking on when you switch the A/C on. Refrigerant work requires special tools and EPA-regulated handling, so if it's low on charge or the compressor isn't engaging, have a shop find and fix the leak rather than just topping it off, since the refrigerant will only leak out again.

title: Puddle of Water Under Car: Normal or Should You Worry?
h1: Puddle of Water Under Your Car? Usually Nothing to Worry About
metaDescription: Clear water under your car after running the AC? Learn when a water puddle is totally normal A/C condensation - and the few times it actually signals a problem.
intro: A clear, odorless puddle of water under your car - especially toward the front passenger side after running the air conditioning - is almost always harmless condensation from the A/C system. As the A/C cools humid cabin air, water collects on the cold evaporator and drains out under the car, exactly like droplets forming on a cold glass. The key is making sure it's actually clear water and not a colored or oily fluid, which would point to a real leak.

commonCauses.detail: By far the most common cause. Running the A/C produces clear water that drains out under the passenger side near the firewall. A puddle the size of a dinner plate or smaller, especially on hot, humid days, is completely normal.
Water is a byproduct of combustion. On cold starts or short trips you may see clear water dripping from the tailpipe or pooling at the rear - harmless and a sign the engine is running efficiently.
Running the defroster or heater in cold, damp weather can also produce small amounts of condensation that drains outside the cabin.
Rainwater and snowmelt drain from the windshield cowl, sunroof channels, and door drains; after rain or a car wash you may see clear water released under the car.
A cracked windshield washer reservoir or hose leaks thin, often slightly blue or colored fluid that can be mistaken for water; check whether your washer fluid level is dropping.

commonCauses.cause: Coolant or A/C leak inside the cabin (the rare concern)
commonCauses.detail: If the 'water' is colored, sweet-smelling, or oily, or if you find dampness on the interior carpet, it may actually be coolant (heater core) rather than condensation and should be checked.

whatToDo: In most cases this needs nothing at all - if the fluid is clear, odorless, and appears only after running the A/C or in damp weather, it's just condensation. To be sure, dab the puddle with a paper towel: clear and watery is fine, while green/orange/pink (coolant), red (transmission), or brown/black and oily means it's not water and needs attention. Only worry if you smell a sweet odor, find wet carpet inside the car, or see colored fluid - in those cases have it inspected.
